newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Workers fight Renault plans, Church weighs in.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Workers fight Renault plans, Church weighs in.

text.p: Angry Renault car workers staged brief strikes in several countries on Friday as the fallout over plans to close a large Belgian plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs spread, while Spain halted subsidies to the company.

Belgian workers took their protest to the French embassy in Brussels, where they hurled the chassis of a Renault car made at the doomed Vilvoorde factory over police barricades to chants from the crowd of "Renault Stays Open".

In Spain, the government shied away from the controversy and said it had decided to freeze a subsidy of two billion pesetas ($13.8 million) it earmarked to top up Renault investment in the modernisation of a plant producing the Clio model in Valladolid.
Renault has run into a storm of staff, union and political protest since revealing its plan last week to shut the plant at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, but is sticking to its decision.
The Catholic Church weighed in, too, on Friday, saying the closure and job losses highlighted the human cost of cut-throat economics and competition, offering advice from the Bible.
"Treat others as you would like them to treat you," said a joint statement issued by the conference of French and Belgian Catholic Churches, quoting the Gospel of Saint Luke.
Renault's Paris headquarters said a trade union call for a string of one-hour work stoppages in Spain and France had not caused any serious disruption.

A spokeswoman said between a quarter and a third of staff had followed strike calls in France, depending on the plant. The biggest stoppage was in Seville in southern Spain, where turnout was about two-thirds.
Renault in Spain gave higher figures for strike turnout at Palencia and the plant in Vallodolid, where Renault plans to spend 12.5 billion pesetas and is counting on state aid.

Asked about Spain's subsidy freeze, an industry ministry spokesman told Reuters: "The Spanish government has taken this decision because it doesn't make any sense for Spain that such a small amount of aid...becomes the centre of controversy".
Renault Spain boss Juan Antonio Moral said the "suspension was exclusively temporary" and the government had assured him the modernisation project would continue to have its support.

Belgian workers at the Vilvoorde plant have downed tools since the firm announced the closure last week. Staff at other car makers in Belgium protested in sympathy on Friday and Renault dealers gave support by closing their doors.

Despite the outrage and condemnation in Belgium -- from the workers up to Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, whose political base is in Vilvoorde -- Renault boss Louis Schweitzer said the withdrawal was necessary, if traumatic.
"The reality is harsh but it's the reality," he said. "If we do nothing, the company will die. It's a brutal, hard and painful decision," he told Europe 1 radio.
Renault also plans 2,700 job cuts in France and Schweitzer said restructuring should go no further.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has asked Schweitzer to meet Belgian staff representatives as soon as possible and a meeting of the company's European works council of employers and employee delegates has been scheduled for next Tuesday in Paris.
The unions are planning a further demonstration that day.
Renault's share price, which soared from 130 francs to 147 francs the day after the closure announcement, has been hit as investors worry about the political risks to the closure plan.
The share held relatively steady on Friday, ending the day on the Paris stock exchange down 0.07 percent at 139.7 francs.
